title: Making beeswax wood finish
subtitle: A hard-wearing natural finish from hive by-products.
excerpt: Beeswax mixed with a carrier oil makes a food-safe, natural wood finish that feeds the grain and builds a soft sheen with each coat. It suits wooden utensils, chopping boards, and bare or stripped furniture. Makes about 200 ml from one batch, enough for a kitchen full of wooden spoons.
sourceNotes: British Beekeepers Association, Using Beeswax (BBKA factsheet). NBU Beekeeper's Toolkit (2024), section on hive products. Rendering Beeswax from Comb, BBKA Practical guide.

glossaryTerms.definition: A hard, natural wax secreted by honeybees and used to build comb. Melts at around 62–65°C. Yellow from pollen-stained comb; bleached white from filtered cappings wax.

content.text: melted into raw linseed or coconut oil and poured into a jar to set. Applied cold and buffed in, it protects wood without sealing the grain or leaving a plastic film. One tin lasts for months of regular use on a working kitchen.
200 ml raw linseed oil (for furniture and external wood) or coconut oil (for food-contact surfaces)
A heatproof bowl, a pan of simmering water, a 250 ml glass jar with a lid
Grate or shave the beeswax into the heatproof bowl. Small pieces melt faster and more evenly.
Set the bowl over a pan of barely simmering water. The beeswax melts at around 62°C. Keep the water well below boiling to avoid overheating the wax.
Once the wax has fully melted, take the bowl off the heat and stir in the oil. The ratio is 1 part wax to 2 parts oil by weight. More wax makes a harder, stiffer paste; less makes a runnier finish.
Pour immediately into the clean glass jar before it begins to set. It sets within a few minutes of cooling below 40°C.
Leave the lid off until the finish has set fully and cooled to room temperature. Then seal and label with the date.

Apply a thin coat with a lint-free cloth, working it into the grain. Leave for ten minutes, then buff vigorously with a clean dry cloth. The heat from buffing melts and spreads the wax into the wood surface. Repeat after the first coat has soaked in fully, usually the next day.

For chopping boards and wooden utensils, use the coconut-oil version and renew the finish whenever the wood starts to look dry. Raw linseed oil finishes on furniture cure over several weeks as the oil oxidises and hardens in the wood fibres.

Raw linseed oil is food-safe when fully cured and suits boards and utensils. Boiled linseed oil contains metallic drying agents and is not food-safe. For furniture and exterior wood use boiled linseed; for anything that touches food use raw linseed or coconut oil.
